title: Prince William ‘blindsided’ by Harry, Meghan return as Kate fears new turmoil from royal feud: experts
summary: Prince William was reportedly "blindsided" by the Sussexes' U.K. return, with royal experts saying he and Princess Catherine are concerned about the fallout.
story: Dan Wakeford, founder of Celebrity Intelligence, discusses Prince Harry's expected UK return, his relationship with King Charles, and why a meeting with Prince William remains unlikely.
Prince William was reportedly "blindsided" by Prince Harry and Meghan Markle’s surprise decision to return to the U.K. with their children.

Several royal experts told Fox News Digital that the Prince and Princess of Wales are "concerned" about the Duke and Duchess of Sussex returning for an extended period beginning this month. Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet are set to begin school there in September, People magazine reported.
"Prince William was blindsided," Kinsey Schofield, host of YouTube’s "Kinsey Schofield Unfiltered," told Fox News Digital.
PRINCE HARRY, MEGHAN MARKLE’S UK MOVE PUTS FRESH SPOTLIGHT ON THEIR EXPLOSIVE CLAIMS AGAINST ROYAL FAMILY

Prince William, Prince of Wales, Catherine, Princess of Wales, Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex leave after escorting the coffin of Queen Elizabeth II to Westminster Hall from Buckingham Palace for her lying in state, on Sept. 14, 2022, in London. Royal experts told Fox News Digital the brothers haven't spoken since 2022. (Emilio Morenatti - WPA Pool/Getty Images)

"He had found Harry’s recent eagerness to publicly signal that he wanted to spend more time in Britain unusual, but that is very different from anticipating a full return. William now has to navigate a situation he did not create, did not ask for and, given the state of their relationship, almost certainly would not have chosen."
A Kensington Palace spokesperson told Fox News Digital: "We would never comment on private family matters."
Prince William, Prince of Wales, Duke of Rothsay and Prince George of Wales attend a service at Crathie Kirk Church on Aug. 23, 2026, in Crathie, Aberdeenshire. (Peter Summers/Getty Images)

In a statement shared with The New York Times, a spokesperson for the Sussexes said, "On the heels of a wonderful trip with family and friends this summer, Harry and Meghan have decided to spend an extended period in the U.K. this autumn. They are excited to have their children spend more time in the country that’s such an important part of their family’s story."
Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, speaks at Scotty's Summer Festival at Maxstoke Castle near Birmingham, central England, on July 11, 2026. (Heathcliff O'Malley/AFP via Getty Images)
The spokesperson confirmed that the couple’s businesses will remain unchanged and based in the U.S. Meghan and Harry will also keep their home in California.
British broadcaster and photographer Helena Chard told Fox News Digital that the Waleses are "feeling uneasy" about facing another chapter in the "endless Sussex soap opera."
WATCH: PRINCE WILLIAM UNLIKELY TO RECONCILE WITH PRINCE HARRY SOON: EXPERT

"It’s about broken trust," Chard explained. "Prince William is said to feel that Harry and Meghan have spent years attacking the institution, then monetizing their grievances through a very lucrative media operation. From his view, it’s an ongoing campaign for maximum impact and self-gain. He’s not going to fuel it, and he’s not going to endorse behavior he sees as damaging."
Prince William, Prince of Wales, and Catherine, Princess of Wales, arrive for a service at Crathie Kirk Church in Crathie, Aberdeenshire, on Aug. 23, 2026. (Jeff J Mitchell/Getty Images)

William and Kate were seen arriving in Scotland on Thursday, where they’ll spend time with King Charles at Balmoral Castle. The royal family has spent summers at the Scottish estate since the reign of Queen Victoria, with family members traditionally hunting, fishing and horseback riding there.
The king learned about Harry and Meghan’s move three days before it was made public, according to reports.

King Charles III inspects the Balaklava Company, 5th Battalion, The Royal Regiment of Scotland, at the gates of Balmoral as he takes up summer residence at the castle on Aug. 18, 2026. (PA Images via Getty Images)

"Prince William, along with Catherine, is currently at Balmoral Castle visiting the king," royal broadcaster Neil Sean told Fox News Digital. "Harry and Meghan have, so far, not been invited to visit the king privately while on a holiday. This will not happen while William is there. I’ve been told he has no desire to connect on any level with his younger brother and simply has no time for [Meghan]."

A spokesperson for Archewell, which handles the offices of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, told Fox News Digital: "We do not comment on the family’s private travel arrangements or meetings with the extended family."

Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, attend the David Foster Foundation 40th Anniversary Celebration on Aug. 7, 2026, in Victoria, British Columbia. (The David Foster Foundation via Getty Images)

The Daily Mail reported that the king and his heir held a "Sussex Summit" following the announcement. A source told the outlet that the Prince and Princess of Wales "have no interest in engaging with anything Harry and Meghan do or say."

Balmoral Castle in Scotland. (Tim Graham Photo Library via Getty Images)

"Things are projected to be tense at Balmoral," British royal expert Hilary Fordwich told Fox News Digital. "... Princess Catherine is particularly guarded given how deeply hurt she was by both of them. Both she and Prince William are very determined to maintain their own family stability and remain focused on duty with their royal roles paramount."
Several royal experts previously told Fox News Digital that William and Harry haven’t been on speaking terms since at least 2022.

From left: Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, Prince William and Princess Catherine watch a Royal Air Force flypast from the balcony of Buckingham Palace on July 10, 2018, in London. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

"My sources have described genuine concern within the Wales camp," Schofield said. "I don’t think Prince William and Princess Catherine are sitting at Balmoral panicking about Harry and Meghan returning, but they are understandably apprehensive about what their return could bring. The last several years have taught them that private family tensions have a habit of becoming very public."
King Charles III and Queen Camilla attend a service at Crathie Kirk Church on Aug. 23, 2026, in Crathie, Aberdeenshire. (Peter Summers/Getty Images)

"The concern isn’t simply that Harry and Meghan will be geographically closer," Schofield continued. "It’s the unpredictability that comes with the Sussexes. There have been interviews, books, documentaries and very personal allegations about members of the royal family. … My sources tell me the Wales camp has not forgotten the hostility directed at them after some of Harry and Meghan’s previous public accusations."
Schofield said unnamed sources told her Kate is also unsettled by the news.

Meghan Markle told Oprah Winfrey in 2021 that Kate Middleton made her cry during a disagreement over flower girl dresses ahead of her wedding to Prince Harry. Meghan said Kate later apologized and brought her flowers and a note. (Chris Jackson/WPA Pool/Getty Images)

"My sources tell me that Catherine does not want to revisit that chapter of her life," Schofield explained. "She has endured very personal allegations, an enormous amount of public scrutiny and a difficult few years. My understanding has always been that her priority is Prince William, their children and the future."

Prince William and Catherine, Princess of Wales attend the 2026 EE BAFTA Film Awards at The Royal Festival Hall on Feb. 22, 2026, in London. (Samir Hussein/WireImage/Getty Images)

"Meghan returning to Britain doesn’t mean Catherine suddenly has an obligation to reopen a relationship that has caused considerable hurt," she said. "Catherine can wish Harry and Meghan well without wanting them back inside her private life. ... The idea of resurrecting the ‘Fab Four’ is fantasy. Too much has happened, and too much has been lost."
The Sussexes are expected to live at a private, nonroyal residence outside London, The Associated Press reported. They won’t resume their royal duties, which they gave up in 2020.

Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex are seen greeting members of the public at the Cruising Yacht Club of Australia on April 17, 2026, in Sydney, Australia. (Cameron Spencer/Getty Images)

The couple’s return to the U.K. comes as the king continues treatment for an undisclosed form of cancer diagnosed in 2024. In 2025, Harry said he didn’t know "how much longer my father has" and expressed a desire for his children to get to know their grandfather.

Prince William (pictured here) did not meet with his estranged younger brother, Prince Harry, who spent time with their father, King Charles III, at Highgrove House, the monarch's private residence, on July 10, 2026. (Chris Jackson/Getty Images)
Last month, the king met with Harry, Meghan and their children at Highgrove House.
Vanity Fair royal correspondent Katie Nicholl reported at the time that, according to sources, "not even the Prince and Princess of Wales were made aware that the meeting was taking place."

"The Sussexes played a blinder with the king welcoming them, having not told him last month of a plan they have had for ages as their children will soon be in school," royal expert Richard Fitzwilliams told Fox News Digital.

"Since the brothers haven’t spoken in years, the imminent arrival of the Sussexes places William and Catherine in a pressured and difficult situation," said Fitzwilliams. "William is reportedly furious. But what is essential is that the king accepts that the Waleses and their children are the future of the monarchy."
Schofield doesn’t believe reconciliation between the brothers is likely, at least anytime soon.

Prince Harry (left) and Prince William (right) attend the unveiling of a statue of their mother, Princess Diana, at The Sunken Garden in Kensington Palace, London on July 1, 2021, which would have been her 60th birthday. title: Kacey Musgraves divides fans with immigrant children’s plea, faces boycott calls to ‘shut up and sing’
summary: Kacey Musgraves asked fans to donate to the Young Center for Immigrant Children's Rights during her tour opener, sparking a divided reaction on social media.
story: Mickey Guyton said she "loves" both Reese Witherspoon and Kacey Musgraves and enjoyed working with them on the show "My Kind of Country."
Kacey Musgraves is facing backlash after asking fans to donate to an immigrant children’s rights group as her birthday wish while kicking off her "Middle of Nowhere" tour.

On Friday, the country music star marked her 38th birthday on the opening night of her tour at the United Center in Chicago, Illinois. At one point, Musgraves paused her show and urged concertgoers to contribute to the Young Center for Immigrant Children's Rights.

"It’s a wonderful organization, and they help give aid — legal aid — and money to children whose parents have been deported unfairly," Musgraves said. "It’s not a political thing. It’s just, these kids need help."

Kacey Musgraves sparked backlash on social media after asking fans to donate to an immigrant children’s rights group as her birthday wish during the opening night of her new tour. (Getty Images for Coachella)

She continued, "They have no guidance and no way to get through this thing without their homebase or their parents. So anyway, 50 cents, whatever the hell, I don't know, whatever you want to do but that would mean a lot to me."
KACEY MUSGRAVES FACES BOYCOTT CALLS AFTER ASKING FANS TO DONATE TO IMMIGRANT CHILDREN'S GROUP
"If you don't want to, that's totally fine too," Musgraves added.

The eight-time Grammy Award winner's appeal was immediately met with applause and cheers from the crowd in Chicago. However, Musgraves' request drew a divided response online, including criticism from conservative political commentators.
The country star said the Young Center supports children "whose parents have been deported unfairly." (Christopher Polk/Billboard via Getty Images)
"What is an unfair deportation?" Tomi Lahren, host of Outkick's "Tomi Lahren Is Fearless" podcast, wrote on X alongside a video of Musgraves' birthday request.
KENNY CHESNEY TELLS BILL MAHER THE KEY REASON HE REFUSES TO TELL HIS LISTENERS HOW TO VOTE

"Kacey Musgraves stopped her concert to ask the audience to donate money for legal aid to kids whose parents have been deported ‘unfairly.’ How about donating money the help kids who's parents have been killed by illegal immigrants! What happened to the country music industry?" conservative influencer Vince Langman commented.
"Another TRAITOROUS woman who wants nothing more than to see our country fall," an X user chimed in.
"Shut up and sing Kasey (sic)!! Why do musicians think they Can draw a line in the sand? You alienate 50% of your audience," another commented.
Some critics declared that they would no longer support Musgraves and called for a boycott of her music and concerts.
NATALIE MAINES’ ANTI-TRUMP TIRADE, ZACH BRYAN’S FENCE-CLIMBING CLASH FUEL COUNTRY MUSIC’S BIGGEST FEUDS
"You just earned yourself a big ol’ boycott, you traitor," one detractor wrote. "Illegal aliens and their kids don’t deserve our patronage and neither do you!"
"I’m deporting Musgraves from all my music playlists," another X user commented.
Critics slammed Musgraves' comments while her fans defended her. (Christopher Polk/Dick Clark Productions via Getty Images)
Other social media users argued that Musgraves should donate her own money rather than ask fans to contribute.

"Kacey Musgraves is worth $15 million. Yet she’s asking fans who already paid $150 to $350 for tickets to donate to support the children of illegal aliens," one social media user commented. "If she cares that much, she can fund it herself and let them live in one of her multi-million-dollar mansions."
MUSICIAN KENNY CHESNEY'S REFUSAL TO SPEAK OUT ON POLITICS SPARKS ARGUMENT ON 'THE VIEW'

"Everyone she is speaking too (sic) gave her their money when they bought tickets," another added. "She did not give the audience money. So now she has the money, shouldn't she donate to whatever cause she wants? She is actually on stage at a show that the audience had to pay to get admission to and now she is asking for more of their money. That's rude."
However, some of the "Dry Spell" singer's fans defended her on social media and praised her for speaking out on behalf of immigrant children.
POP STAR OLIVIA RODRIGO FELT 'ENRAGED' AFTER ICE USED HER HIT SONG, BRANDS AGENCY 'BARBARIC'
"Love this. 'It's not a political thing. It's just, these kids need help.' Exactly. More artists doing this please," one fan wrote on X.

"In all fairness, the kids didn’t do anything wrong," another wrote. "I don’t believe their parents were wrongfully deported, but I equally believe that their children, if retained in the United States by law, should be taken care of. We’re not f------ animals!"
"No boycott here!" an X user declared.

"Helping children caught in difficult circumstances is a worthy cause," one commenter argued. "At the same time, immigration enforcement and whether a deportation was lawful or justified are matters for the courts and policymakers not concert stages."
Fox News Digital has reached out to Musgraves' representatives for comment.
Musgraves stood by her support for the organization following the concert.  (Dan MacMedan/Getty Images)
Meanwhile, Musgraves stood by her remarks on social media, taking to her Instagram Story to upload a post that read, "Kinda chic when kids don't face immigration court alone."
The singer also reposted a message shared by the Young Center's Instagram page, in which the organization expressed its gratitude to her.
"Thank you," the nonprofit wrote. "We appreciate your support of our work and mission to see unaccompanied immigrant children safe, free, and with their families."

Based in Chicago, the Young Center describes its work as pairing volunteers with attorneys and social workers to advocate for unaccompanied and separated immigrant children in government custody. Its website lists family unity, release from custody, fair proceedings and children's best interests among its priorities.

The nonprofit reported serving 1,975 children from 53 countries in 2024 and opening 1,388 new cases. Its 2025 annual report said children's average detention time increased from 30 to 198 days and requests for assistance from detained parents quadrupled from 2024.

Friday’s appeal extended Musgraves’ support for the charity. In April, resale platform Depop announced that 20 pieces from her wardrobe, including clothing from music videos and tours, would be sold in capsule drops. Women's Wear Daily reported that all proceeds would benefit the Young Center.
In announcing the sale, Musgraves described the beneficiary without discussing immigration enforcement.
The eight-time Grammy Award winner wrote "Kinda chic when kids don't face immigration court alone." (Taylor Hill/Getty Images for ABA)
"I also adore the fact that the sales are supporting a really beautiful cause," Musgraves said.

Musgraves also invited three brothers, ages 18, 14 and 12, to open three Texas shows in May after their family was released from ICE custody. The mariachi performers' family said they entered through the now-defunct CBP One appointment system in 2023 and sought asylum after fleeing violence in Mexico, KSAT reported.

DHS said the family entered illegally and had been released into the country by the Biden administration. Responding to the family’s detention, DHS said federal law required custody while its immigration claims were heard.

"The law requires illegal aliens who show up at a port of entry without valid entry to be detained while all their claims are heard. You can look it up in the statute," a DHS spokesperson told KSAT. "Unlike the previous administration, the Trump administration is not going to ignore the rule of law."
Musgraves previously invited a trio of brothers to open three Texas shows in May after their family was released from ICE custody. (Joseph Okpako/WireImage)

Musgraves' latest remarks came as ICE enforcement reached record levels. Federal sources told Fox News Digital that agents made about 51,000 immigration arrests in July, topping the previous record of roughly 43,000 in June.

"Every day, the brave men and women of ICE are arresting and DEPORTING dangerous criminal illegal aliens, including gang members, from our country," DHS said.

title: Mariska Hargitay nearly left 'Law & Order SVU' over fear of being a 'one-trick pony'
summary: Mariska Hargitay revealed she once told Julianna Margulies she needed to leave "SVU," but her blunt response changed everything.
story: Dennis Quaid spoke out about receiving the 2026 Patriot Ally Award at the 2nd Annual Military & Veteran Entertainment Awards Gala.
Mariska Hargitay once considered leaving "Law & Order: Special Victims Unit" after more than two decades as Olivia Benson because she worried the role had come to define her career.
In a new interview with Variety, the actress — who has starred as Benson since "SVU" premiered in 1999 — said she began questioning her future on the long-running NBC drama around its 25th season.
"I’ve got to leave the show too. I don’t want people to think I’m a one-trick pony," Hargitay recalled telling "ER" co-star Julianna Margulies.
'THE BIG BANG THEORY' STAR JIM PARSONS SAYS HE PAID A STEEP PRICE FOR FAME
Mariska Hargitay explained why she nearly quit "Law & Order: SVU" during a new interview with Variety. (Getty Images; Michael Schwartz for Variety)
Margulies, who famously left "ER" after six seasons, had a blunt response.
"Sweetheart, that ship’s sailed," Hargitay said Margulies told her.
While Benson made her a household name, the Emmy winner admitted she often felt constrained creatively due to the grueling production schedule.

"The comedy thing was painful to me because I felt like I was only exercising one part of myself," Hargitay said. "People would say, ‘You need to get off that show and do comedy. You need to get off that show and have a talk show.’"
‘X-FILES’ STAR GILLIAN ANDERSON REVEALS PARENTING REGRET, SAYS SHE WISHES SHE WAS 'LESS SELFISH'
Hargitay has portrayed Olivia Benson since 1999. (Jose Perez/Bauer-Griffin/GC Images)

"I wasn’t ready to leave, because I loved it," she said. "And then I got to do all this other stuff, and that’s why I don’t think about leaving right now. Do I want to quit now? No. Why? I made a movie while shooting; I did a play for six weeks on hiatus. I’m hosting the Emmys."

"Dick Wolf is truly a visionary," she said Tuesday. story: The legendary actor's wife and daughter told Fox News Digital the focus on his weight was "upsetting," but that he handled it well.

"We will remember Shelley for her kindness, loyalty, wit, courage, and beautiful spirit. We will miss her deeply — not only as a celebrated performer, but as the loving and extraordinary person she was in our everyday lives," they added.

Fabares became one of television's most recognizable young stars when she was cast as Mary Stone, the teenage daughter of the characters played by Donna Reed and Carl Betz, on "The Donna Reed Show" in 1958.
During her time on the hit family sitcom, Fabares unexpectedly launched a successful recording career after the show's producer, Tony Owen, decided to incorporate singing into the series.

The actress' debut single, "Johnny Angel," reached No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1962 and sold more than 1 million copies. She released several albums and scored additional hits with "Johnny Loves Me" and "The Things We Did Last Summer," though she later acknowledged that she never considered herself much of a singer.

Fabares left "The Donna Reed Show" as a regular cast member in 1963 but returned for guest appearances before the series ended in 1966. She remained close to Reed, whom she credited as a mentor who helped her navigate Hollywood as a young actress.

Donna Reed and Shelley Fabares are pictured with baseball player Don Drysdale of the Los Angeles Dodgers in an episode of "The Donna Reed Show." (Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)
At the height of her teen idol fame, Fabares transitioned to the big screen and starred opposite Elvis Presley in three movies: "Girl Happy" in 1965, "Spinout" in 1966 and "Clambake" in 1967.
She also appeared in the 1964 surf movie "Ride the Wild Surf," the 1966 musical comedy "Hold On!" with Herman’s Hermits and the 1968 Hank Williams Jr. film "A Time to Sing."

Born Michele Ann Marie Fabares on Jan. 19, 1944, in Santa Monica, California, she was the niece of actress Nanette Fabray. Fabares began modeling as a young child and made her television debut at age 10 on an episode of "Letter to Loretta."

Her early credits included appearances in "The Bad Seed," "Never Say Goodbye," "Jeanne Eagels" and "Marjorie Morningstar." She also appeared with Annette Funicello in the 1958 Disney serial "Annette."

After her initial success as a teen star, Fabares built a prolific television career that spanned several decades. In 1971, she portrayed Joy Piccolo, the wife of Chicago Bears running back Brian Piccolo, whom James Caan played, in the acclaimed television movie "Brian's Song," which also starred Billy Dee Williams.
Elvis Presley and Shelley Fabares starred in the 1967 film "Clambake." (Getty Images)

Fabares later held regular roles on "The Brian Keith Show," "The Practice" and "Forever Fernwood." From 1978 to 1984, she played Francine Webster, the professional rival of Bonnie Franklin’s Ann Romano, on "One Day at a Time."
She also made guest appearances on television shows, including "The Twilight Zone," "Mannix," "The Rockford Files," "The Love Boat," "Fantasy Island," "Mork & Mindy" and "Murder, She Wrote."
MACKENZIE PHILLIPS SAYS SHE AND VALERIE BERTINELLI DRANK WINE, DID COCAINE DURING SITCOM BREAKS

In 1989, Fabares found renewed success when she joined the ABC sitcom "Coach" as Christine Armstrong, the girlfriend and eventual wife of Hayden Fox, the college football coach played by Craig T. Nelson.

Fabares remained with the series throughout its nine-season run, appearing with Craig T. Nelson, Jerry Van Dyke and Bill Fagerbakke until the show ended in 1997. Her performance earned her two Emmy nominations for Outstanding Supporting Actress in a Comedy Series, in 1993 and 1994.
'MIRACLE ON THE HUDSON' HERO CAPTAIN 'SULLY' SULLENBERGER REVEALS ALZHEIMER'S DIAGNOSIS
Shelley Fabares starred as Christine Armstrong on "Coach" from 1989 to 1997. (Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)

Later in her career, Fabares lent her voice to Martha Kent in several animated Superman projects, including "Superman: The Animated Series," "Justice League" and the 2006 film "Superman: Brainiac Attacks."

Fabares became an advocate for Alzheimer's awareness after her mother, Elsa, was diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease. She helped raise money for research, delivered speeches and testified before Congress about the disease. Her mother died in 1992.

In 1999, Fabares faced a serious health crisis when doctors discovered she had progressive liver failure related to autoimmune hepatitis. After spending nearly two years on a transplant waiting list, she had a liver transplant in October 2000.
Shelley Fabares remained married to "M*A*S*H" actor Mike Farrell for more than 40 years until her death. (Getty Images)

title: Motown songwriter behind 'Money (That's What I Want)' and other hits dead at 87
summary: Janie Bradford Hobbs co-wrote "Money (That's What I Want)" with Berry Gordy and penned hits for Marvin Gaye, Stevie Wonder and The Supremes.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

Janie Bradford Hobbs, an early Motown songwriter who co-wrote "Money (That’s What I Want)" and penned songs recorded by Marvin Gaye, Stevie Wonder and other music legends, has died after an extended illness at 87.
Bradford Hobbs died at a Los Angeles hospital, her family said Saturday.
Born in Charleston, Missouri, Bradford Hobbs later moved to Detroit, where neighbor and singer Jackie Wilson introduced her to Motown founder Berry Gordy in the late 1950s.
COMMODORES CO-FOUNDER AND FORMER BASSIST RONALD LAPREAD DEAD AT 75
Janie Bradford attends the Mary Wilson tribute at The GRAMMY Museum on March 4, 2022, in Los Angeles, California. (Emma McIntyre/Getty Images)

She started working for Motown as a receptionist in 1958, but her role soon went well beyond answering phones. Like many employees in Motown’s early days, Bradford Hobbs became involved in making the music.
She and Gordy wrote "Money (That’s What I Want)," which Barrett Strong recorded in 1959. The song became one of Motown’s first hits and was later recorded by The Beatles.

Bradford Hobbs also wrote "Too Busy Thinking About My Baby." The Temptations recorded the song first, and Marvin Gaye later had a hit with it. She also wrote songs for Stevie Wonder, The Supremes, Martha & The Vandellas and others.
Janie Bradford, left, and George Clinton attend a ceremony honoring Clinton with a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame, Jan. 19, 2024, in Los Angeles. (Richard Shotwell/Invision/AP, File)
"Janie was there with me from the very beginning, before there was even a Motown, and she will always hold a very special place in my heart and in the Motown family," Gordy said in a statement.
COUNTRY MUSIC ICON DON SCHLITZ, WHO WROTE KENNY ROGERS' HIT 'THE GAMBLER,' DEAD AT 73
Gordy described Bradford Hobbs as one of the people who believed in Motown before anyone knew what it would become.

"Janie was one of a special group I have always thought of as the original Motown family — the unsung heroes who believed in the dream before anyone knew what Motown would become," Gordy continued. "She was one of the people who helped make Motown what it became."
Janie Bradford attends The Paley Center For Media Hosts A Legendary Evening With Mary Wilson at The Paley Center for Media on Feb. 25, 2019 in Beverly Hills, California. (Leon Bennett/Getty Images)

Bradford Hobbs later became head of Writer Relations for Jobete, Motown’s publishing company. After leaving Motown, she founded the annual Heroes and Legends Awards, which honored figures in the music industry and awarded scholarships for about 30 years, according to her family.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
She is survived by her husband, Wardean Hobbs; daughter, Nicole Hobbs; son, Lance Finney; and two grandsons. Funeral arrangements have not been completed.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: FDA approves once-daily pill for deadly cancer after patients' survival rates nearly double
summary: Revolution Medicines' Rasonque targets the RAS protein driving 95% of pancreatic adenocarcinoma cases, offering a critical option after chemotherapy fails.
story: An experimental pancreatic cancer vaccine shows promise in its first human trial, generating an immune response in 90% of high-risk patients.
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved the use of a new cancer treatment pill Wednesday.

Rasonque, manufactured by Revolution Medicines in California, is an inhibitor for the most common type of pancreatic cancer. The tablet, which is taken once daily, targets multiple forms of a protein called RAS that drives tumor growth.
In a press release, the FDA called Rasonque a "new treatment option for patients with advanced pancreatic cancer," noting the agency approved it more than six months ahead of its review deadline.
CANCER TREATMENT DELAYS SURGE ACROSS US AS DOCTOR WARNS SYSTEM ‘NEEDS FIXING IMMEDIATELY’

"Today’s approval provides a critical new option for patients facing an extraordinarily difficult and historically hard-to-treat cancer. It is our fundamental duty to deliver more cures and meaningful treatments to patients as quickly as possible," acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas said in a press release.
"I am immensely proud of the dedicated FDA scientists whose fast, thorough review and relentless commitment made this groundbreaking milestone a reality."
Taken as a once-daily tablet, Rasonque directly inhibits multiple forms of the RAS protein, which acts as the main driver of tumor growth in pancreatic cancer. (iStock)
The authorization is for adults with metastatic pancreatic cancer that either did not respond to at least one prior treatment or could not receive certain combination drug therapies.

Pancreatic adenocarcinoma remains one of the deadliest forms of oncology in the U.S., accounting for up to 95% of the roughly 67,000 annual pancreatic cancer cases identified by the National Cancer Institute.
PATIENTS REMAIN CANCER-FREE NEARLY 3 YEARS AFTER RECEIVING EXPERIMENTAL IMMUNOTHERAPY
While the disease makes up only 3.2% of total cancer diagnoses, it causes a disproportionately high number of cancer deaths because it is often found late and can spread quickly.

The new drug was approved after a randomized, open-label trial of 500 patients with pre-treated metastatic disease. Patients taking Rasonque achieved a median overall survival of 13.2 months, nearly double the 6.7-month survival rate seen in the standard chemotherapy control group.
The FDA approved Revolution Medicines' Rasonque 6½ months ahead of schedule for adults with previously treated or multiagent-ineligible metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma. (Revolution Medicines)
"This drug showed unprecedented results in an area of high unmet need," said Angelo de Claro, M.D., director of the FDA’s Oncology Center of Excellence.

Regulators accelerated the medication's path to market by granting it priority review, orphan drug status and a breakthrough therapy designation.
Additionally, the filing was evaluated using the FDA commissioner’s National Priority Voucher pilot program to speed up access to critical public health treatments.

Ahead of the official green light, the agency issued a "safe to proceed" letter in May, opening an expanded access protocol that allowed patients to receive the drug before final approval.
The most frequent side effects reported during clinical trials included rash, diarrhea, stomatitis, nausea, fatigue, vomiting, abdominal pain, edema, reduced appetite and hemorrhage. (iStock)

Safety profiles show that the most frequent adverse events linked to Rasonque included rash, diarrhea, mouth sores (stomatitis), nausea, fatigue, vomiting, abdominal pain, fluid retention (edema), reduced appetite and bleeding (hemorrhage).

title: Dolly Parton’s private cancer battle highlights why some patients don’t share their diagnoses
summary: Dolly Parton kept her cancer diagnosis private before her death, raising questions about why some patients hide their health battles and the stigma involved.
story: Dr. Kristin Higgins, chief clinical officer at City of Hope Cancer Center in Atlanta, surmised that Dolly Parton may have preferred for people to remember her for her ‘amazing career’ and not for a diagnosis at the end of her life.
Dolly Parton’s death on Tuesday followed a brief bout with cancer, according to statements from her family.

"After bravely facing a brief battle with cancer, Dolly departed her Earthly life today at the Vanderbilt-Ingram Cancer Center surrounded by loved ones," the family shared, as confirmed by Fox News Digital.

The revelation of the singer’s previously undisclosed cancer battle is raising questions about why some patients choose to keep a diagnosis private, even as public figures’ health struggles can spark wider awareness.
DOLLY PARTON DEAD AT 80

Dr. Kristin Higgins, chief clinical officer at City of Hope Cancer Center in Atlanta, surmised that Parton may have preferred people remember her for her "amazing career" and not for a diagnosis at the end of her life.
Keeping the disease private at first is a "very natural response," Higgins said, as a diagnosis can be very overwhelming.
Dolly Parton’s death on Tuesday followed a brief bout with cancer, according to statements from her family. (Getty Images)
"It's very natural to cling to that identity of being a healthy, vibrant person without a diagnosis of cancer," Higgins told Fox News Digital.
"The patient really needs to acclimate to the idea of themselves having this disease and then start to tell friends and family kind of slowly after they go through that adjustment process."
CANCER TREATMENT DELAYS SURGE ACROSS US AS DOCTOR WARNS SYSTEM ‘NEEDS FIXING IMMEDIATELY’
In some cases, people may withhold a cancer diagnosis due to a feeling of shame or embarrassment, Higgins said.

"Things like tobacco-related cancers, unfortunately, still carry a stigma when diagnosed," she said. "Patients may feel that it was their fault. And the reality is nobody deserves a cancer diagnosis."
An oncologist surmised that Parton may have preferred for people to remember her for her "amazing career" rather than for a medical diagnosis at the end of her life. (Getty Images)
There are some benefits, however, to eventually sharing a cancer diagnosis with friends, family and community members who can rally around the patient, according to the doctor.

"For example, for people who are religious, letting their greater circle know about that diagnosis can be really helpful, as people will pray for them as they're going through the journey of treatment," Higgins said.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"I think, overall, it's a very beneficial thing to eventually tell as many people as possible so you can get that support."
The doctor also agreed that sharing a cancer journey can raise awareness and provide support to others facing the same challenge.
"It's very natural to cling to that identity of being a healthy, vibrant person without a diagnosis of cancer."

"If you are somebody with a cancer diagnosis, and you're beating it, and you are going through treatment successfully, other people seeing that — whether it's on social media or hearing it through a friend — that can be really helpful to an individual as they're facing a new cancer diagnosis," Higgins said.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Another benefit of disclosing cancer is that it may open up more opportunities for treatments.
"There are so many resources out there now. … Clinical trials are really what move the needle in the cure rates for cancer, and finding out about these trials is not easy," Higgins noted.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"So, the more people who know about your diagnosis — you have all these cheerleaders out there rooting for you, and you can get more information. You can hear more people's opinions about where you could seek the best cancer treatment."
"Our statistic is that 70% of people diagnosed with cancer will survive five years or more," said an oncologist.  (iStock)
The doctor said there's more hope than ever for people facing a cancer diagnosis.

"Our statistic is that 70% of people diagnosed with cancer will survive five years or more," she said. "And we can do it, we can get through it.
"I think … the beauty of sharing this diagnosis with the world is that we can get all the support we need."

title: Eating less of common ingredient early in life may slash cancer risk decades later
summary: Researchers found that early-life sugar rationing in post-war Britain correlated with lower cancer risk and slower aging roughly 50 years later.
story: Dr. Brian Slomovitz of Mount Sinai Medical Center explains why reducing excess sugar may help curb inflammation and support cancer prevention, while stressing that balance matters more than extreme diets or completely avoiding favorite foods.

Limiting sugar consumption during the first 1,000 days of life, from conception through a child’s second birthday, may result in slower biological aging and a lower risk of cancer up to five decades later.

A study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences investigated how early-life sugar intake influences health in adulthood, examining data from over 64,000 participants in the UK Biobank born between 1951 and 1956.
The researchers leveraged a natural experiment from post-war Britain, when sugar rationing ended in September 1953.
DIRTY SODA DRINKS ARE EVERYWHERE, BUT DOCTORS WARN OF HEALTH RISKS: 'METABOLIC DISASTER'

After rationing ended, average daily sugar consumption across the U.K. nearly doubled — from about 41 grams to 80 grams — while consumption of other major foods remained stable, according to historical National Food Survey data cited in the study.

People exposed to sugar rationing during their first 1,000 days of life were compared to those who were conceived after the policy ended. Researchers then examined cancer outcomes recorded about five decades later.

Researchers examined over 64,000 UK Biobank participants by leveraging the abrupt end of British sugar rationing in September 1953, which caused adult sugar intake to nearly double while other foods remained stable. (iStock)
They found that people who spent more of their early lives under sugar rationing had lower rates of several cancers in adulthood, including liver, rectal, lung, prostate and breast cancers.

People exposed to early sugar limits also had longer leukocyte telomeres — protective caps on chromosomes that tend to shorten with age — equivalent to about two fewer years of biological aging. They also had lower levels of Granzyme B, a protein associated with long-term immune activation and inflammation.
EATING COMMON DAIRY FOOD EVERY DAY MAY SLOW BIOLOGICAL AGING, STUDY SUGGESTS
The study’s authors identified two key pathways that could explain these long-term benefits: a biological imprint and a persistent behavioral habit.
Five decades after rationing ended, adults who spent their earliest days under sugar restrictions were still consuming less sugar and eating healthier, more varied diets.
Consuming less sugar during pregnancy and the first years of life may lower the risk of developing cancer decades later, the study suggests. (iStock)
Experts said the findings add to ongoing research into how early diet may influence long-term health, though further research is needed to confirm the connection.
"What surprised me most was how persistent the effects were," study author Weilong Zhang of the University of Cambridge told Fox News Digital.
POPULAR DAILY DRINKING HABIT COULD NEARLY TRIPLE RISK OF DEADLY CANCER, MAJOR STUDY FINDS

"We might expect childhood diet to matter for health, but differences in sugar exposure during just the first 1,000 days were still reflected in people's diets and biological markers roughly five decades later."
"This suggests that early life may be an especially important period not only for biological development, but also for establishing long-lasting food preferences."

"We might expect childhood diet to matter for health, but differences in sugar exposure during just the first 1,000 days were still reflected in people's diets and biological markers roughly five decades later," the researcher said. (iStock)
Dr. Brian Slomovitz, deputy director of the Sylvester Comprehensive Cancer Center at Mount Sinai Medical Center in Miami Beach, described the research as an "excellent hypothesis-generating study."

"Sugar consumption is something that we have been worrying about ... most importantly, inflammation, and how inflammation can lead to some cancers," Slomovitz, who was not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

High sugar intake has been linked to metabolic disruption, insulin resistance and chronic inflammation, which may contribute to disease risk, according to Dr. Marc Siegel, senior medical analyst for Fox News.
Siegel said the lower cancer rates were consistent with the possibility that less early sugar exposure and healthier later-life diets played a role.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
However, outside oncologists note that natural experiments from decades past come with inherent research limitations.

"We're talking about the 1950s, so clearly there are some biases in data collection," Slomovitz noted. "Secondly, the numbers are very, very, very low. Of all the cancers, most of them had [fewer] than 100 cases ... to show a 70% decrease, I think is probably an ambitious conclusion."
Individuals with longer early-life exposure to sugar rationing experienced reduced adult incidence rates for liver, rectal, lung, prostate and breast cancers. (iStock)

The doctor also pointed out that while obesity-driven cancers align with metabolic pathways, other findings in the paper — such as reduced lung cancer risk — are traditionally tied to external factors like smoking rather than dietary sugar.
The researchers noted that, as a natural experiment rather than a randomized trial, the study could not rule out all other postwar factors.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Additionally, the UK Biobank is not fully representative of the broader British population, and the researchers could not determine how much of the effect reflected early biological changes versus healthier diets maintained in adulthood.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Zhang cautioned against overinterpreting the findings as a reason for extreme dietary measures.

"I would not interpret our study as saying that parents should eliminate sugar completely," he said. "Rather, our findings support existing recommendations to limit added sugar, particularly during pregnancy and early childhood."
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: Deadly measles outbreak hits Northeast as state records first deaths in 35 years
summary: Two unvaccinated Lancaster County residents died from measles, marking Pennsylvania's first measles deaths in 35 years amid 393 confirmed cases.
story: Senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel discusses the critical link between low MMR vaccination rates and surging measles cases in states like Utah and South Carolina. He emphasizes the vaccine's safety and role as the only tool to prevent the highly contagious disease.
Pennsylvania confirmed two measles-related deaths on Tuesday, according to the state’s department of health.
This marks the first losses related to the highly contagious virus within the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania in 35 years.

The Pennsylvania Department of Health (DOH) confirmed that both Lancaster County individuals were unvaccinated, noting that the best way to prevent measles infection is to get the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine.
MEASLES SURGE HITS NEW MILESTONE AS US CASES SURPASS LAST YEAR'S TOTAL
The MMR vaccine administered over two doses can boost a person’s immune system and provide 97% lifetime protection, according to health officials.
Two deaths have been confirmed in Pennsylvania related to measles. (iStock)
In a press release, Pennsylvania Secretary of Health Dr. Debra Bogen shared her "deepest sympathies" with the "loved ones who are facing this unimaginable loss."

"Because measles was largely eliminated in the Commonwealth for more than three decades, people are not familiar with this disease and don’t fully understand the potential severity of the illness," she said in the statement. "We want to ensure that every Pennsylvanian has the information they need to protect themselves, their loved ones and their communities."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"As a physician, I want to make sure that people understand the MMR vaccine is safe and provides the best protection we have against measles."
The state's DOH has confirmed 393 cases of measles in 28 counties so far in 2026.
The Pennsylvania DOH has confirmed 393 cases of measles in 28 counties so far in 2026. (iStock)
Measles is a highly contagious virus that can be fatal in one to three patients per 1,000 cases, data shows.
The virus can cause long-term health problems, including pneumonia and brain swelling. Nearly 20% of individuals who contract measles are hospitalized.

Measles spreads when an infected person breathes, coughs or sneezes, spreading the virus through respiratory droplets. It can remain infectious in the air and on surfaces for up to two hours after the person leaves the area, experts caution.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Early measles symptoms include fever, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes. A measles rash follows a few days later, starting on the head and spreading down to the rest of the body.
Symptoms can start seven to 21 days after exposure. Those who believe they were exposed to measles should contact a healthcare provider.
Early measles symptoms include fever, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes. A measles rash follows a few days later, starting on the head and spreading down to the rest of the body. (iStock)
Dr. Jesse Goodman, former FDA chief scientist in Washington, D.C., spoke with Fox News Digital about the MMR vaccine, calling it "extremely safe and highly effective."

"The vaccine prevents millions of measles deaths worldwide annually, including hundreds that used to occur in the U.S.," he said. "There is no evidence that MMR vaccine causes any chronic illnesses, including autism."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Dr. Amesh Adalja, senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security in Baltimore, Maryland, agreed that Pennsylvania's 35-year streak without a measles-related death "wasn't luck."

"It was the vaccine working so completely that an entire generation of parents grew up never seeing what this virus does to a child’s lungs or brain," he told Fox News Digital. "That protection is increasingly not valued, and this is the predictable result when the population turns their back on a life-saving technology."

"The vaccine prevents millions of measles deaths worldwide annually, including hundreds that used to occur in the U.S.," a doctor told Fox News Digital. "There is no evidence that MMR vaccine causes any chronic illnesses, including autism." (Raquel Natalicchio/Houston Chronicle via Getty Images)
Dr. Marc Siegel, Fox News senior medical analyst, previously emphasized the highly contagious nature of measles amid elevated case counts across the U.S.

"Measles is so contagious that up to 90% of susceptible people who are exposed to an infected person will become infected," he told Fox News Digital, stressing the importance of community protection. "We need a 95% vaccine coverage rate to ensure herd immunity," he said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The herd immunity threshold is a mathematical estimate based on how contagious a disease is and how effectively immunity from vaccination or prior infection prevents its spread, according to Siegel.

"In this case, two-dose vaccination is almost 100% effective, and natural immunity after a measles infection is generally lifelong," the doctor said. "This isn’t about personal choice, it’s about community protection. We need to protect those who can’t have a live virus vaccine because they are immunocompromised or pregnant."
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Major brain changes that occur around age 50 could impact dementia risk
summary: Microglia decline after age 50 as inflammatory blood-derived immune cells infiltrate the hippocampus, potentially driving neuroinflammation and dementia.
story: Dr. Daniel Amen — psychiatrist, brain imaging specialist and founder of Amen Clinics in California — says this quick, 15-second method can help calm the body and mind.
The brain may undergo a notable shift at midlife, as new research suggests that its protective immune cells begin to decline and are increasingly replaced by inflammatory cells at around age 50.

Researchers from the University of California, San Diego; New York Genome Center; and University of California, Irvine, found that these brain changes may help explain why aging increases the chances of neuroinflammation and neurodegenerative disease, including dementia.

The study analyzed postmortem tissue from the hippocampus – the portion of the brain that is responsible for learning and memory – in 40 neurologically healthy adults, ranging from 20 to 95 years of age.
THE 'AGE' OF YOUR BLOOD COULD PREDICT DEMENTIA RISK, NEW STUDY SUGGESTS

"The most striking change was that after about age 50, the brain’s resident immune cells, called microglia, appear to be increasingly replaced by immune cells that enter from the bloodstream," first author Nathan Zemke, Ph.D., principal investigator at the UC San Diego Center for Epigenomics, told Fox News Digital.
"Microglia normally protect the brain by clearing debris and responding to injury, but the incoming cells carry stronger inflammatory signals."

The brain may undergo a notable shift at midlife, as new research suggests that its protective immune cells begin to decline and are increasingly replaced by inflammatory cells at around age 50. (iStock)
The researchers believe this shift may contribute to chronic inflammation linked to cognitive decline and neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer’s.

They also noted the deterioration of cells involved in maintaining the blood-brain barrier – the protective filter that helps keep harmful substances out of the brain – as well as widespread changes in DNA and gene activity.
'LONGEVITY GENE' MAY PROTECT THE BRAIN FROM ALZHEIMER'S BY BOOSTING DNA REPAIR, STUDY FINDS

One of the most exciting implications of the study, according to Zemke, is that the replacement immune cells originate in the blood, which means they are more accessible than cells already deep inside the brain.

"It may eventually be possible to modify blood-derived immune cells so that they are more protective and less inflammatory when in the brain," he said. "That could provide an entirely new way to approach Alzheimer’s and other neurological diseases without having to directly manipulate cells within the central nervous system."
Researchers found that these brain changes may help explain why aging increases the chances of neuroinflammation and neurodegenerative disease, including dementia. (iStock)

Although these findings are still in early stages, Zemke said, gaining a better understanding of why this immune-cell replacement happens – and why it happens earlier in some people than others – could lead to new strategies for preserving brain health during aging.
The study’s chief limitation is that it studied human brain tissue collected postmortem from different individuals across the adult lifespan, the researchers noted.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"That allows us to identify strong age-related patterns, but it cannot directly show how the same person’s brain changes over decades or prove that a particular cellular change causes cognitive decline or Alzheimer’s disease," Zemke said.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"We also do not yet know what triggers the influx of blood-derived immune cells into the brain. Determining whether changes in the blood-brain barrier, inflammation, genetics, lifestyle or other factors initiate this process will be an important next step."
The timing and extent of the brain changes varied considerably between individuals, suggesting that brain aging is not necessarily a fixed process that happens identically in everyone. (iStock)
The researcher emphasized, however, that he would not recommend that people make any specific medical or lifestyle changes based on this study alone.
"These findings are primarily about understanding the biology of brain aging and identifying new directions for prevention and treatment," he said.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
The timing and extent of the brain changes varied considerably between individuals, suggesting that brain aging is not necessarily a fixed process that happens identically in everyone.
"The next challenge is to understand what drives that variation and whether some of those factors can be modified," Zemke added.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The study also included a small sample of just 40 people and examined tissue only from the hippocampus, meaning the findings may not reflect immune changes throughout the entire brain.
The study, which was funded by the National Institutes of Health, was published in the journal Science.

title: Anti-aging supplements taken by millions may undermine cancer treatment, study warns
summary: Popular NAD+-boosting supplements like NMN and nicotinamide riboside may shield pancreatic cancer cells from chemotherapy, a new study warns.
story: Family medicine physician Dr. Jessica Gray details a new experimental pancreatic cancer vaccine showing promise in its first human trial. The vaccine, targeting the KRAS mutation, generated an immune response in 90% of high-risk patients. Dr. Gray discusses the 5-7 year timeline for public availability and emphasizes why pancreatic cancer is so deadly, highlighting advances in cancer treatments.
Over-the-counter anti-aging supplements taken by millions of Americans to boost energy and lessen the side effects of chemotherapy may actually impair cancer treatments, a new study suggests.

Researchers at the Case Western Reserve University School of Medicine found that popular vitamin B3 derivatives – including nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), nicotinamide riboside (NR) and nicotinamide (NAM) – could help cancer cells survive chemotherapy.
Those compounds are used by the body to produce NAD+, a molecule that helps cells generate energy and repair damage.
IV THERAPY AND SUPPLEMENTS UNDER SCRUTINY AS EXPERTS WARN OF POTENTIAL SIDE EFFECTS

The study, published in the journal Cancer Letters, examined how these supplements interact with treatments for pancreatic cancer, a particularly deadly form of the disease with a 13% five-year survival rate, according to the American Cancer Society.
Over-the-counter vitamin B3 derivatives, specifically NMN, NR and NAM, could help pancreatic cancer cells survive chemotherapy treatment, the study suggests. (iStock)

While boosting NAD+ levels through dietary supplements can offer health benefits to non-cancerous cells, pancreatic cancer cells may exploit the extra resources to repair damage caused by chemotherapy and avoid cell death, the researchers found.

In both laboratory settings and animal models, the supplements shielded cancer cells against three common chemotherapy drugs: oxaliplatin, 5-fluorouracil and gemcitabine. As a result, tumors survived chemotherapy doses that typically would prove fatal to them.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"Our findings highlight a potentially concerning role for NAD+-boosting supplements in the context of active cancer, especially when used in conjunction with chemotherapy," said study lead Jordan Winter, a professor at Case Western Reserve School of Medicine and co-leader of the developmental therapeutics program at the Case Comprehensive Cancer Center, in the press release.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"Our discovery is a call to action for the medical community."

The study notes that these B3 derivatives are not considered dangerous for healthy individuals using them for general wellness. However, the risk becomes significant for patients currently undergoing active cancer therapy.
Boosting NAD+ levels provides extra energy to cancer cells, allowing them to repair DNA damage caused by chemotherapy. (iStock)
"This research is a critical reminder that ‘natural’ doesn’t always mean safe, especially in the complex biology of cancer treatment," Winter added.

In light of the findings, the research team recommends that oncology teams begin routinely screening patients for supplement use. They also called for more studies into how NAD+ precursors interact with cancer therapies.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Winter urged patients currently in treatment to consult their oncologists before taking any over-the-counter supplements.
Because the study relied on laboratory cell cultures and animal models, the findings may not directly translate to how human patients process these supplements during treatment, the team noted.

The findings indicate these supplements are not inherently dangerous for healthy individuals using them for general anti-aging or wellness, but pose serious risks when taken during active chemotherapy. (iStock)
Additionally, the research focused exclusively on pancreatic cancer, meaning the supplements may not have the same effect on chemotherapy for other cancer types or with different drug combinations.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The study also only evaluated short-term cellular responses under controlled laboratory conditions and not human clinical trials, so it remains unclear how these supplements could affect cancer patients over time.
Fox News Digital reached out to multiple NAD+ supplement manufacturers for comment.
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: 'Perfect' workout formula can take just 10 minutes a day, Hilaria Baldwin says
summary: Hilaria Baldwin shares her "perfect" workout trifecta of cardio, strength training and stretching, plus tips for building exercise consistency.
story: The yoga instructor reveals how she incorporates running, stretching and toning into her routine, while involving her children and modeling the importance of caring for physical health.
Being motivated to work out is one thing, but staying committed to a routine is what yields results, experts say.
In an interview with Fox News Digital, certified yoga and fitness instructor Hilaria Baldwin shared her tips for building an effective exercise routine – and sticking to it.

"One of the most important things about exercise is consistency," said the mother of seven. "For many of us, life gets in the way – we are parents, and we work and all the chaos comes in, so bite-sized movements are really important."
CHIEFS HEIRESS GRACIE HUNT REVEALS WHY SHE LIFTS HEAVY WEIGHTS — AND DOESN’T COUNT CALORIES
Baldwin revealed that her "perfect" workout routine trifecta always includes cardio, strength training and stretching, even if it’s just 10 minutes per day.

For lasting consistency, a fitness routine should fit naturally into one’s lifestyle and schedule, Baldwin said. She recommends setting aside kid-free, work-free blocks of time for movement and self-care.
Hilaria Baldwin joined Fox News Digital for an interview about her "perfect" daily workout routine. (Angelica Stabile/Fox News Digital)

Baldwin said she makes time for a daily run as her cardio, which she said helps "work out her lungs." She also incorporates stretching and strength training, which might include physically picking up her kids or toning with weights.
She has also started exercising with her children as a way to blend family time with physical activity.
DOCTORS SAY 8 FORGOTTEN HABITS COULD HELP FIGHT STRESS, OBESITY AND CHRONIC DISEASE
The instructor emphasized consistency without overcommitment, noting that doing too much, too soon can lead to burnout.

"If something's overwhelming, we're not going to do it," Baldwin said. "Ultimately, we are going to be creatures of habit … we are going do what we feel like needs to get done – but starting to think of a workout more like brushing our teeth is really important."
Hilaria Baldwin demonstrates a deep lunge position during a yoga practice. She says yoga is "amazing" for staying flexible with age. (Angelica Stabile/Fox News Digital)

"People are not moving their bodies enough, and then we get sick," she went on. "So, the question is, can we do a little bit to prevent that? And obviously not everything can be prevented, but we know that we should move our bodies most days."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Baldwin advised against "biting off more than you can chew." For example, instead of running three miles as a response to being frustrated about your fitness goals, try running for just 10 minutes – or run for just two minutes at a time and take walking breaks.
"Doing something is better than thinking about it and doing nothing," she added.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The fitness instructor also suggested making exercise a family commitment, helping to reinforce that movement and self-care are priorities.
"As moms, we [often] put ourselves last," she said. "Everybody says put your oxygen mask on first, but we don't do that."
Hilaria Baldwin demonstrates a side stretch during a yoga sequence. (Angelica Stabile/Fox News Digital)
"I think showing our children that we are human, and we are worth taking care of is really important – not just for our relationship with them, but how they will treat themselves when they're older."
When life gets busy, she said, it’s easy to make excuses for not working out. Baldwin admitted that on most days, especially in the summer heat, she has "zero interest" in going for a run.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"But I know that I'm not going to regret it," she said. "It’s just about creating the habit and saying, ‘Okay, I'm going to do this, and it's going to be 30 minutes, and I might hate it, but I’m going to be happy to do it.’"
Baldwin added, "Showing up is the hardest thing. Once you do it, and you create a commitment, it completely changes everything."
"Showing up is the hardest thing. Once you do it, and you create a commitment, it completely changes everything," said Hilaria Baldwin. (iStock)
'Love yourself'
Baldwin encouraged the public, especially women, to tap into how "special and unique each person’s body is."
"Start loving yourself and loving your body, no matter what outside opinions you feel like people are directing at you," she said. "Feel capable and feel strong and that you're worth investing in."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Baldwin shared that she herself has struggled "tremendously" with this in her own life. "That is one of the reasons that I show up – to tell my body, ‘I love you, you're worth it.’"

She continued, "Nobody has ever existed who is exactly like you, and no one will ever be exactly like you again. So please live every single day cherishing your body, your unique self, and let's have fun and move together."
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Louisiana girl, 8, dies after contracting suspected brain-eating amoeba linked to lake swim
summary: Lillian Smart's family says the 8-year-old's brain injuries were too severe to survive after contracting Naegleria fowleri while swimming in a lake.
story: Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel warns beachgoers about the rise of Vibrio vulnificus, a deadly flesh-eating bacteria found in warm salt waters. Already nine cases reported in Florida and five deaths in Louisiana.

Lillian Smart, an 8-year-old girl who health officials believe contracted a brain-eating amoeba while swimming in a northern Louisiana lake, died Saturday at a Ruston hospital from an infection linked to the pathogen.
Lillian died one day after celebrating her eighth birthday.

"The injuries to her brain were too severe for her little body to recover from," the Smart family said in a statement posted Sunday morning on Facebook. "Everyone did everything they could to keep her here. We are heartbroken and honestly do not know what to do next. How do we put one foot in front of the other without our girl?"
MICHIGAN REPORTS 2 DEATHS IN RARE PARASITE OUTBREAK THAT HAS SICKENED MORE THAN 11,000

The Louisiana Department of Health announced Wednesday that a state resident had been hospitalized after becoming infected with Naegleria fowleri, a microscopic amoeba that can cause a rare and often deadly brain infection.
Lillian Smart, center, is pictured with her parents. The 8-year-old died Saturday after her family said she contracted Naegleria fowleri. (Facebook/Love for Lillian Smart)

State health officials have not publicly identified Lillian as the patient referenced in the announcement. Her family, however, said on social media that she had been admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit at a Ruston hospital and identified Naegleria fowleri as the cause of her illness.
The health department said the infection in the case it announced was most likely acquired while the patient was swimming in Lake Claiborne shortly before becoming ill.
BEACHGOERS WARNED AFTER DEADLY 'FLESH-EATING' BACTERIA KILLS 5 IN SOUTHERN STATE
A representative for the Louisiana Department of Health did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.
Louisiana Department of Health records identify three previous deaths associated with Naegleria fowleri in the state since 2011.
Lillian Smart, 8, died Saturday after her family said she contracted Naegleria fowleri, a rare amoeba that can cause a deadly brain infection. (Facebook/Love for Lillian Smart)

Two happened in 2011. A 20-year-old man in St. Bernard Parish died after using tap water to rinse his sinuses, while a 51-year-old woman in DeSoto Parish died after using tap water for a similar purpose.

In 2013, a 4-year-old boy contracted the amoeba while visiting a home in St. Bernard Parish, where he had played on a slip-and-slide. State officials later reported that CDC testing detected Naegleria fowleri in the parish water system.
DEADLY BACTERIA FOUND IN WATERS NEAR LUXURY VACATION DESTINATION AHEAD OF SUMMER

Naegleria fowleri causes primary amoebic meningoencephalitis, or PAM, an extremely rare brain infection that can develop when contaminated water enters the nose and the amoeba travels to the brain. People cannot become infected by swallowing contaminated water.
The amoeba is not found in saltwater or properly chlorinated swimming pools.
A birthday memory jar invited loved ones to share favorite memories and messages for Lillian Smart ahead of her eighth birthday. (Facebook/Love for Lillian Smart)

Symptoms typically begin with headache, fever, nausea and vomiting before progressing to a stiff neck, seizures and coma. Symptoms generally appear about five days after infection, and the disease can lead to death within about one to two weeks.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
About 97% of people who develop PAM die from the infection, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The CDC reported two PAM cases nationwide last year. Of the 173 infections documented over roughly the past 90 years, nearly 91% occurred in July and August.
Brittany Miller is a Fox News Digital breaking news writer and former Independent reporter who graduated from Syracuse University in 2023.

title: Popular erectile dysfunction drug linked to eye disease that can cause irreversible vision loss
summary: Tadalafil users were 22% more likely to develop glaucoma, a study found, raising new questions about long-term Cialis use and eye pressure risks.
story: Dr. Daniel Amen discusses emerging research showing saffron may be as effective as SSRIs in treating depression, and could also improve sexual function.
A drug used to treat erectile dysfunction and enlarged prostate symptoms may raise the risk of glaucoma, a serious eye condition that can cause gradual vision loss, according to new research.

An international team of researchers analyzed health records from nearly 74,000 men ages 40 and older with lower urinary tract symptoms to examine whether long-term tadalafil use was associated with a greater risk of glaucoma.

The study, published in the British Journal of Ophthalmology, compared about 37,000 men prescribed tadalafil with a similar group who did not use phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors, the drug class that includes Cialis.
Researchers followed the men for up to five years and looked for new cases of glaucoma and high pressure inside the eye, along with whether patients needed treatment for glaucoma.
VISION PROBLEM LEADS TO MAN'S STAGE 4 LUNG CANCER DIAGNOSIS, NEW DRUG EXTENDS SURVIVAL
New research suggests tadalafil, the drug sold as Cialis for erectile dysfunction and enlarged prostate symptoms, may be linked to a higher risk of glaucoma. (iStock)
Men who used tadalafil were 22% more likely to develop glaucoma than those who did not use the drugs, according to the findings.
They were also 32% more likely to develop high pressure inside the eye and 33% more likely to develop primary open-angle glaucoma, the most common type of the disease.
Dr. Valerie Kattouf, an optometrist at the Illinois Eye Institute who was not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital that glaucoma can be difficult to notice in its early stages.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"Glaucoma is an eye condition that especially in its early stages often does not present with visual symptoms," Kattouf said.
As glaucoma progresses, people may gradually lose their side, or peripheral, vision, she said.
The study found that men who used tadalafil were 22% more likely to develop glaucoma than men who did not take the drug. (iStock)
"Clinical findings of glaucoma are best detected in a comprehensive vision evaluation," Kattouf added.

Kattouf said people with a family history of glaucoma, high pressure inside the eye or severe nearsightedness may face a higher risk. Those who take Cialis daily over a long period of time may also warrant closer monitoring, she said.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

People who regularly use the medication should have a comprehensive eye exam to establish a baseline for their eye health, according to Kattouf. Doctors can check pressure inside the eyes and perform other tests to look for changes that could signal glaucoma.
The researchers noted several limitations to the study.
People who take the medication regularly should get a thorough eye exam to establish a baseline for their eye health. (iStock)
The study was observational, meaning it found a link between tadalafil use and glaucoma but could not prove that the medication caused the condition.
Researchers also could not account for changes in medication use or other health conditions that developed over time.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The researchers stressed that the findings do not mean people should stop taking tadalafil. Instead, they said, patients who use the medication long term, particularly those with existing glaucoma risk factors, may benefit from regular eye monitoring.
Fox News Digital reached out to Eli Lilly, the manufacturer of Cialis, and the study’s researchers for comment.
Kelly McGreal is a production assistant with the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

title: Men face new pressure to stay ‘hot’ as they age — and it’s not just about living longer
summary: Plastic surgeon Dr. Krishna Vyas reveals why men no longer feel stigma around cosmetic procedures and shares the foundational steps for extending "hotspan."
story: The stigma around men seeking esthetic treatments is fading. For many, the goal isn’t to look younger, it’s to make their appearance feel more aligned with how youthful, confident and socially engaged they feel.
Maintaining healthy cholesterol and blood pressure, along with regular physical activity, are widely recommended components of healthy aging.

But as interest in longevity grows, some older adults are looking beyond extending their healthspan — the number of years lived free of disease — to prioritize looking, feeling and remaining physically attractive as they age.
Experts say the desire to maintain one’s appearance — the pursuit of "hotness" — can be psychological, shaped in part by a disconnect between how people feel and the changes they see in the mirror.
COULD 'HUMANMAXXING' ACTUALLY HELP YOU LIVE LONGER? HERE'S WHAT EXPERTS SAY
"It really isn't about age," Dr. Krishna Vyas, M.D., Ph.D., a plastic surgeon at Blechman Plastic Surgery on Fifth Avenue in Manhattan, told Fox News Digital.

"I think it's when you look in the mirror and you're like, 'I don't recognize myself. I don't recognize the way I feel. I don't identify with how my appearance isn't concordant with how I feel at that point.'"
The push for aesthetic interventions is often driven by psychological friction when a person's mental self-image no longer matches their physical appearance, experts say. (iStock)
Men now account for roughly 15% of all cosmetic procedures, according to data from the American Society of Plastic Surgeons.
Social barriers that may have previously prevented men from seeking aesthetic treatment have diminished in the last two decades, Vyas noted.

"In the past, there was a stigma ... men were once shamed or ashamed of seeking out things that improve their appearance, especially in aesthetics, but that barrier has fallen significantly," he said.
DO RED LIGHT THERAPY AND COLD PLUNGES REALLY WORK? A DOCTOR REVEALS THE TRUTH

The motivations driving men to pursue "looksmaxxing" — a social media term for enhanced efforts to improve physical appearance — range from maintaining a competitive edge in youth-centric workplaces to addressing subtle signs of aging, such as dark under-eye circles or loss of jawline definition, according to Vyas.
Treatments range from minimally invasive procedures like Botox and laser therapy, to surgical interventions like chest masculinization and liposuction.
Men now represent roughly 15% of cosmetic procedure patients, driven in part by workplace competitiveness and a decline in the historical stigma surrounding aesthetic treatments. (iStock)

"The misconception often is that minimally invasive treatments will fix things and have no side effects," Vyas cautioned, noting that improper or excessive non-surgical treatments can change the normal layers and contours of facial tissue.
5 steps to looking your best
Before jumping to aesthetic procedures as quick-fix substitutes for biological health, the surgeon recommends taking the following steps to improve physical appearance.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Complete abstinence from all forms of nicotine is essential to maintaining microvascular circulation and preventing premature skin breakdown, according to Vyas.
Experts warn that minimally invasive cosmetic treatments are not risk-free fixes and can distort underlying tissue if overused. (iStock)

Avoid over-hyped trends and multi-step routines, the experts recommended. Guidelines from the American Academy of Dermatology point to two daily essentials: a morning broad-spectrum sunscreen to block photoaging UV rays, and a topical retinoid at night to stimulate cell turnover.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Maintaining a healthy weight can prevent the chronic, systemic inflammation that is linked to metabolic syndrome, which directly accelerates structural skin and tissue aging.
Aesthetic procedures cannot substitute for internal wellness, making things like daily sun protection and early hair loss intervention crucial first steps. (iStock)

Intervene early at the first sign of thinning. Evidence-based medical treatments, like FDA-approved finasteride and minoxidil, remain the primary standard for maintaining hair density before follicle loss becomes permanent.
"The real longevity drug is exercise — aerobic and non-aerobic strength training exercises," Vyas said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Someone who's looking for a hotspan or a healthspan, because they're so intimately related … I think they should focus on the basics to start ... the foundation is what's most important," the surgeon added.
